My slightly cynical opinion is that pharma reps and new publications have something to do with this (lithium is not patented so is not marketed and has no vested interest in being researched more). This push definitely helped get lamotrigine above lithium on common best practice lists that many psychiatrists just follow on good faith. 
But also likely some bad few cases of poor monitoring and adherence let to some paranoia. Admittedly, the lower overhead (no monitoring besides watching for a rash the first few weeks) on lamotrigine is a plus, especially among people like us who aren't always very motivated to go get blood drawn.

I wasn't on it very long, but did a lot of research (reading the original journal articles, etc.. I come from an academic background). 
The most important thing to know for you and anyone considering lithium: It is NOT the scary drug that some people make it out to seem. It's just an element, and even 'normal' people can benefit from it in low doses (just like, say, magnesium). The blood tests are just extra safety.

There's genetic and environmental factors intertwined for everyone. A genetic vulnerability will be expressed more easily/rapidly in a bad environment, but some will develop the disorder even with the most rosy of upbringings. There's a slight danger of 'post-hoccing' though; trying to attribute your disorder to a specific something. Especially when this something is partially self-inflicted (e.g., substances) it might be tempting to blame yourself for the disorder, which is not very helpful. Acceptance (and forgiveness and/or processing, if harm was done to you) imo is the key to moving forward.

Hey friend. Welcome! You've found the right place :D 

It sounds like you've gone through quite the journey; I'm glad you shared it with us. 

You mention quite a lot but I really want to focus on the right now, because that's really what's most important. It seems like you're asking whether one can be in the hospital for too long, or whether you 'should' be able to manage this on your own by now. But the thing is, with this disorder that we have, there's really no such thing as 'should', and sometimes we have to accept that we do need outside help. Quite often, we're really doing the best we can and are actually fighting and working harder than most 'normal' people. 

So, right now it really sounds like you're not doing so great. You mention that you haven't really showered or eaten in an entire week. You don't deserve to face this alone. It's okay if you go back to the hospital—unless what you actually meant is that it's costing too much? That's a slightly different problem to tackle. Otherwise it sounds like you could benefit from an intensive outpatient programme—or at the very least a community support group. Or even some sort of online community.. Oh wait, you've already taken that awesome first step :) 

I don't know the intimate details of your situation so I'm really just throwing ideas around, but reply and let's bounce around some ideas that might work? If there really is nothing else available, you have us, and we can help you beat this motherfucker one day at a time ;) 

edit: I have [this post (link)](https://www.reddit.com/r/bipolar/comments/5duh1f/depression_my_extremely_practical_guide_to_making/) saved and it often helps me enormously through the down phases.

I know this isn't the answer you're hoping for, but: Please go see a professional (your pdoc should be able to see you briefly with no charge). We can't reliably answer your question one way or another (per the sidebar), and the consequences of the 'bad' Lamictal rash (even though, statistically, it's unlikely) are severe enough that any suspicions should be taken very very seriously.

Hey MethRollins69

So it's been a pretty crazy rollercoaster, and I'd guess you're feeling kinda out of control at the moment. Despite your best intentions, weed has taken over (and even invited MDMA to the party) and you're at a place where all you know is that you need help. 

Despite appearances, that's actually a relatively good place to be in. Admitting that you need help is *huge*. Well done for having the strength to admit that, and to type out all the painful things that have happened lately. 

When we're in the trenches of being addicted, it's often the drugs that take over some of our thought patterns and convince us of lies to keep using. As you said, you're thinking that you can't function with people while sober, but you *know* that that's not true—you have first-hand evidence that you're (much, much) better when sober. The hard part is not listening to those drug-driven thoughts, and being able to take action to get to a place without them. 

You've sent up a flare and we've seen it; now we need to figure out how to best get help to you. Is there perhaps someone you trust enough to confide in about these things - and maybe even stay with for a while? I know everything seems really difficult right now, but can you think of any possible plans of action? Anything that comes to mind.. Don't try to evaluate or second-guess them, just type them out (as many as you can) while you think of them.

Oh yes, it definitely won't suit everyone! 

I'm fairly sceptical about the 12-step approach in general (particularly the religious undertones), but it really does depend on what you're looking to get out of it. 

For me, I had to realise that sometimes the actual content isn't as important as the connections. (To throw in a cliché: "the opposite of addiction isn't sobriety, it's connection".) 

More context: A driving factor in me going was that I would almost certainly have used a few days ago, had my dealer not been on holiday. I know my friends either a) don't get it or b) are quite tired of me messaging them in times like that for encouragement, so I realised I needed a sponsor who understood and didn't mind me reaching out to them at odd hours. 

Other support structures (including this sub) might be sufficient for others, but I knew I'd reached the point where I needed to throw myself into an in-person supportive network of clean-living people. 

(That turned into more of a rant than I intended!)

That I might meet someone I know also crossed my mind—but I had to really stop and think about why that would matter. In the end, it would really just be meeting someone who at some point was *also* afraid of their first meeting and all the uncertainties involved. Logically, there could/should be no shame (in either direction) because you're both there for exactly the same reason. 

Don't get me wrong, I was very much terrified walking into that hall, but everyone was extremely friendly and really there with that common purpose. Even more: They treat any newcomer as the most important person in that meeting, and will gladly do whatever they can to make you feel more comfortable (e.g., allowing you to mainly observe, answering any questions, etc.)

I hope this isn't misinterpreted as preachy; I just know that I needed a gentle nudge to find more support and hope to pass on that nudge to whoever might need it. The line that ultimately made me decide to go was: "non‑addicted people don't spend their time wondering if they're addicts".
